_comment: Polynesian expansion batch 173 - Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4: Story of Islands' Formation and Origin of Race (Kahakuikamoana mele, pp. 2-9); Story of Umi (birth, pp. 178-186); Story of Lonoikamakahiki (konane games, pp. 274-292). Topics 1 creation, 4 founding legends, 3 heroic tales. All passages are labeled paraphrase.

title.en: Wakea and Papa Bear the Islands of Hawaii
title.zh: 瓦基亞與帕帕誕生夏威夷群島

region.zh: 夏威夷群島（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Hawaiian tradition recorded by Fornander from Kahakuikamoana; published 1916-1917

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Story of Islands' Formation and Origin of Race (Honolulu 1916-1917)

texts.license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: According to the traditions of Wakea and his wife Papa these islands were the real children of this pair: Hawaii was the first child of Papa and Wakea, and some time afterwards Maui was born, and in this manner there were successive births of eleven islands. Kahoolawe alone was not born of Papa and Wakea but, according to the legend of Haumea, Hina gave birth to this island. The mele of Kahakuikamoana sings each island's birth - Molokai from Kuluwaiea of Haumea and Hinanuiakalana; Lanai a foundling; Oahu a wohi through Ahukinialaa; Kauai a kingly scion; Niihau, Kaula and Nihoa the three children of Wanalia and Hanalaa born in the same day, after which the mother conceived no more.
summary.zh: 瓦基亞與帕帕的傳說中，這些島嶼是他們真正的兒女：夏威夷是長子，其後毛伊誕生，如是相繼產下十一島。唯有卡霍拉維非二人所出，而是哈烏梅亞傳說中海娜所生。卡胡伊卡莫阿納的歌詠各島誕生——摩洛凱出自哈烏梅亞之子庫魯瓦埃亞與希娜努伊阿卡拉納；拉奈為拾孤；瓦胡經阿胡基尼阿勞而為沃希之島；考愛為王裔之嗣；尼豪、考拉與尼豪阿乃瓦納利亞與哈納拉同日所生三子——此後母親再無孕身，群島不再添新。

sensitivity.note: Islands-as-children cosmogony; the mele also weaves in Kamehameha's name-song feats.

passages.text: There are twelve islands in this group and they are situated in the Pacific Ocean to the north of the Equator and between latitude 18 degrees 54 minutes and 22 degrees 17 minutes, in west longitude 154 degrees 54. The wise people are not all agreed as to the origin of these islands, and some have thought that they appeared or grew up from the sea; but according to the history of Hawaii the ideas of the learned historians were entirely different from that theory. According to the traditions of Wakea and his wife Papa these islands were the real children of this pair, being born of Papa and having Wakea for their father: Hawaii was the first child of Papa and Wakea, and some time afterwards Maui was born, and in this manner there were successive births of eleven islands. But Kahoolawe was not born of Papa and Wakea, but according to the tradition or legend of Haumea, Hina was the one who gave birth to this island and it was called Kahoolawe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Story of Islands' Formation (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then arose Hawaii-nui-a-kea, arose from inside, from the inner darkness; then appeared the island, the land, the row of islands of Nuumea, the group of islands on the borders of Tahiti. Maui was born an island, a land, a dwelling place for the children of Kamalalawalu. Kuluwaiea of Haumea as the husband, of Hinanuiakalana as the wife, was born Molokai, a god, a priest, the first morning light from Nuumea. Here stands the king, the heavenly one, the life-giving water-drops from Tahiti: Lanai was found, an adopted child. Uluhina then was called upon, the navel of the little one was cut, the afterbirth of the child that was thrown into the folds of the rolling surf, the froth of the heaving sea - then was found the loin cloth for the child. Molokini the island is the navel string; the island is the navel string. Now stands forth Ahukinialaa, a chief from the foreign land: then was born Oahu, a wohi, a wohi through Ahukinialaa. Then was born Kauai, a chief, a prince, a kingly scion of the chiefly cluster belonging to Hawaii - Hawaii the foremost head of the islands that was spread out by Kalani.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Kahakuikamoana mele (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Wanalia was the man and Hanalaa was the woman; of them was born Niihau, a land, an island, a land at the roots, the stem of the land. There were three children among them, born in the same day: Niihau, Kaula, ending with Nihoa; the mother then conceived no more - no island appeared afterwards. It is Kalani who consecrates the islands, exalted in Nuumea among the royal cluster of Kaialea; the thirds were joined together by Kalani: Hilo, and Puna, and Kau were thrown in. According to this song composed by Kahakuikamoana the historical legend of the derivation of these islands is explained, and it seems it was from Tahiti that the first people of this race came, though it is not made plain by the lines of this song. The notes add that Wakea and Papa as here shown are the traditional creators of nearly all the islands of the Hawaiian group; other legends refer to this pair as the progenitors of the Hawaiian race, and from Wakea sprang the line of chiefs while the second son, Lihau-ula, is stated as founding the priesthood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Kahakuikamoana mele (1916-1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Umi, Born of the Chief Liloa and the Commoner Akahi

region.zh: 夏威夷島哈馬庫阿懷皮奧谷

texts.period: Hawaiian tradition; recorded by Fornander; published 1916-1917

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Story of Umi, chs. 1-3 (Honolulu 1916-1917)

texts.license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: King Liloa, travelling to Puna, meets the beautiful commoner Akahiakuleana just as her defilement-days are over, and leaves his royal malo with her as a pledge. She bears Umi in Waipio and raises him humbly; when the boy's quarrels reveal his parentage, the malo identifies him and Liloa takes him to court, outranking his legitimate son Hakau - the seed of the tragedy that Umi will later avenge.
summary.zh: 利洛阿王巡遊普納，邂逅平民美人阿卡希阿庫萊阿納——正值其穢期方過；臨別以王室腰帶相贈為信物。她在懷皮奧誕下烏米，含辛茹苦將其撫養；孩童鬥毆暴露身世，腰帶證實其為王裔，利洛阿攜其入宮，位在嫡子哈考之上——日後烏米報仇的悲劇由此埋下伏筆。

sensitivity.note: Royal-bastard founding legend of the Umi dynasty.

passages.text: King Liloa, travelling to Puna, meets the beautiful commoner Akahiakuleana just as her defilement-days are over, and leaves his royal malo with her as a pledge of his return. Akahiakuleana gives birth to Umi, and the genealogical tree of the child traces him to the king; the defilement-days of Akahiakuleana being just over at the meeting, the boy grows up in humble circumstances, ignorant for years of the father whose token he keeps.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Story of Umi (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Umi's boyhood quarrels reveal his parentage, the royal malo identifies him and Liloa takes him to court, placing him above his legitimate son Hakau - the seed of the tragedy that Umi will later avenge. The beauty of Akahiakuleana is emphasized in the tradition as 'a very beautiful woman', and the phrase ola na iwi, the life of the bones, marks the humble circumstances of Umi's upbringing among the commoners before the malo disclosed his royal blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Story of Umi (1916-1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Lonoikamakahiki Wins at Konane and Is Called Liar
title.zh: 洛諾伊卡馬卡希基棋盤上的智勇

region.zh: 瓦胡島凱魯瓦（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Hawaiian tradition; recorded by Fornander; published 1916-1917

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Story of Lonoikamakahiki (Honolulu 1916-1917)

texts.license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: Sailing to Oahu, Lonoikamakahiki contests with King Kakuhihewa - konane (Hawaiian checkers), first one game then the second to fifth contests, and finally the wager over the hiding place of the bones of the chiefs slain by Keawenuiaumi. Winning each trial, Lono reveals the secret grave and returns to Hawaii to deal with his rebellious chiefs, leaving Kakuhihewa shamed at the board.
summary.zh: 洛諾伊卡馬卡希基航行瓦胡，與卡庫希黑瓦王連番較藝：先弈黑白棋一局，繼而二至五局，最後賭上被克瓦維努伊阿烏米所誅酋長骸骨的藏匿之處。連連得勝後，洛諾揭出祕葬之地，返夏威夷平服叛臣——留給卡庫希黑瓦的只有棋盤前的羞辱。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legendary king cycle; konane contest record.

passages.text: Sailing of Lono to Oahu, and the arrival of Ohaikawiliula: Lono's contest with Kakuhihewa, then the wager made by Kakuhihewa against Lono, and the second to fifth contests, with the arrival of Kaikilani - Lonoikamakahiki proving his worth at the konane board, the Hawaiian checkers, game after game against the king of Oahu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Story of Lonoikamakahiki (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The dispute between Kakuhihewa and Lono about the hiding-place of the bones of the chiefs slain by Keawenuiaumi ends with Lono revealing the secret grave - how Lono revealed the bones of chiefs slain by Keawenuiaumi being the eighth chapter of his story. Winning each trial Lono returns to Hawaii, where Kaikilani, the first chiefess ruler, receives him, and together they deal with the rebellious chiefs at Napoopoo - the exploits of the great soldier of victories, who conquered Oahu at the games if not on the field.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Story of Lonoikamakahiki (1916-1917); not verbatim.

region.zh: 瓦胡島凱魯瓦（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Hawaiian chant tradition; recorded by Fornander; published 1916-1917

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, History of Kualii (Honolulu 1916-1917)

texts.license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: The song of Kualii, repeated by Kapaahulani, celebrates the Oahu chief's character and doings: his genealogical tree traced from Kane to Wakea, his battles and battle-grounds, his trip to Hawaii, his return to Oahu from Molokai, and the battle fought at Kalakoa - a favorite residence at Kailua where he died, aged, and full of honours.
summary.zh: 由卡帕阿胡拉尼傳唱的庫阿利伊之歌，頌揚瓦胡酋長的生平戰功：其族譜自卡內上溯至瓦基亞；戰場遍歷，遠征夏威夷，自摩洛凱返瓦胡，以及卡拉科阿之役——晚年居凱魯瓦而終，享盡尊榮。

passages.text: Kualii's character and doings are sung in the chant repeated by Kapaahulani, with a supplementary chant for Kualii, and his genealogical tree traced from Kane to Wakea: the battles of Kualii and the battle grounds, the trip to Hawaii, the return to Oahu from Molokai, and the battle fought by Kualii at Kalakoa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, History of Kualii (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kailua, Oahu, was the favorite residence of Kualii, where the bearer of the feather cloak would disappear to, where he set out from and returned on his way; Kualii died at Kailua, aged and full of honours - the great soldier of Oahu whose feats in arms are enumerated in the chant, and whose name the mele of Kumu Honua compares with the Vikings of the Pacific.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, History of Kualii (1916-1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Moikeha Returns from Tahiti to Kauai
title.zh: 莫伊克哈自塔希提出航返考愛

region.en: Kauai to Tahiti and back (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 考愛至塔希提往返（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Hawaiian tradition; recorded by Fornander; published 1916-1917

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, History of Moikeha (Honolulu 1916-1917)

texts.license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: Driven to Tahiti by the slander of Luukia, Moikeha sojourns there and builds the temple and palace Lanikeha; homesick, he answers the mele of Kamahualele that proclaims 'O, Moikeha, the chief who is to reside', and sets sail for Hawaii. He lands and takes the rule of Kauai, marrying the twin chiefesses who fell in love with the handsome voyager, and fathers the Kila line whose youngest son will be sent back to Tahiti to avenge his father's wrongs.
summary.zh: 受盧基亞讒言所迫，莫伊克哈遠走塔希提，居留其間築廟建宮——蘭尼凱哈；思鄉之情隨卡馬胡阿萊勒的頌歌湧起：『看哪，莫伊克哈，將要定居的酋長！』他揚帆返夏威夷，登陸即得考愛之政，娶下戀慕這俊偉航海者的雙生女酋，而其幼子基拉日後將重返塔希提為父雪恥。

sensitivity.note: Moikeha cycle; Kamahualele's mele named in the tradition.

passages.text: Moikeha, after a sojourn in Tahiti, returns to Hawaii: the slander of Luukia - who heard cheering and was told Moikeha was defaming her - drove him from his home; Mua was the betrayer of Moikeha, sowing discord between Luukia and him. In Tahiti he built the temple and palace Lanikeha, his home; and when the chant of Kamahualele sounded in his honour, 'O, Moikeha, the chief who is to reside; O Moikeha is the chief', he ceased from his ease and set sail from Tahiti for Hawaii.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, History of Moikeha (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Moikeha's residence on Kauai followed his arrival: he became chief of Kauai and the twin chiefesses fell in love with him on landing - Laamaikahiki could be found later only through the prophecy spoken in the presence of Kila. Moikeha's bones would one day be brought back from Haena by his descendants; his son Kila, the youngest and favored, would be sent to Tahiti to slay Moikeha's enemies, avenge his father's wrongs and succumb to Luukia - so the cycle of the restless voyager closes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, History of Moikeha (1916-1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Lono and the Bones beneath the Root

region.zh: 夏威夷島科納海岸（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Hawaiian tradition; recorded by Fornander; published 1916-1917

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Story of Lonoikamakahiki (Honolulu 1916-1917)

texts.license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: The dispute between Kakuhihewa and Lono about the hiding-place of the bones of the chiefs slain by Keawenuiaumi is settled when Lono, who had been entrusted with the secret as a boy, points out the tree whose roots grew through the grave; the digging proves him truthful, and the wager of konane, lands and lives is paid - the bones of the slain restored to their people and Lono's name established as the knower of hidden things.
summary.zh: 卡庫希黑瓦與洛諾就被誅酋長骸骨藏處打賭；自幼受託守密的洛諾指出樹根穿墳之處——掘之果然，賭約以棋局、土地與性命償清；亡者遺骨歸還族人，洛諾『通曉隱祕者』之名亦由此奠定。

passages.text: How Lono revealed the bones of chiefs slain by Keawenuiaumi is the eighth chapter of the story: the dispute between Kakuhihewa and Lono about the hiding-place of the bones was settled when Lono, who had been entrusted with the secret as a boy, pointed out the tree whose roots grew through the grave; the digging proved him truthful, and the wager of konane, lands and lives was paid - the bones of the slain restored to their people and Lono's name established as the knower of hidden things.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Story of Lonoikamakahiki (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The contests with Kakuhihewa - konane, the wager, the second to fifth contests with the arrival of Kaikilani - had already marked Lono out among the chiefs of Oahu; when the dispute of the bones was joined to these, Kakuhihewa had wagered against Lono all that a king could stake, and the revelation of the grave won it all for the visitor from Hawaii.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Story of Lonoikamakahiki (1916-1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Kepakailiula, the Stranger Who Cut the King in Two
title.zh: 客卿克帕卡伊烏拉斬王之戰

region.zh: 毛伊島哈納（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Hawaiian oral tradition; recorded by Fornander; published 1916-1917

source.work: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kepakailiula (Honolulu 1916-1917)

texts.license: Public domain (Bishop Museum Memoirs vol. IV, 1916-1917)

summary.en: Makolea, daughter of Kakaalaneo, sails to Kauai and becomes wife of Kaikipaananea, one of the three strong men of Oahu; Kukaea, who lived on filth, throws his rival into the oven. Kepakailiula, the avenger, lands in Hana where King Kakaalaneo - an expert spearsman with two spears - meets him; the spear attacks fail and the king is cut in two by the war-club of Kepakailiula, his last breath naming the stranger's parentage.
summary.zh: 卡卡拉內奧之女瑪科萊阿航至考愛，嫁與瓦胡三大力士之一的卡伊基帕阿納內阿；以穢物為食的庫卡埃亞將其情敵投入大灶。復仇者克帕卡伊烏拉登陸哈納；善使雙矛的卡卡拉內奧王親自迎戰——矛攻無功，王竟被克帕卡伊烏拉的戰棍攔腰斬為兩段，臨終道破來客的出身。

sensitivity.note: Revenge-quest episode of the Kakaalaneo cycle.

passages.text: Makolea arriving at Kauai becomes wife of Kaikipaananea, one of the three strong men of Oahu, in boxing beaten by Kepakailiula and in wrestling matches; Kukaea, who lived on filth, threw Kaikipaananea into the oven, and Kepakailiula, befriended by a high chief under Kaikipaananea, came to avenge him - Kepakailiula befriended by the high chief who sheltered him in Kauai.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kepakailiula (1916-1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kakaalaneo, an expert spearsman, holding two spears, meets Kepakailiula; Hana is filled with chiefs and men ready to fight for him, and he fails in his spear attack on Kepakailiula - he is cut in two by the war-club of Kepakailiula, the avenger's blow answering the king's spear, and the kingdom of Hana left without its master.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Folk-lore, vol. 4, Legend of Kepakailiula (1916-1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Ua the Rain and the_origin of War

source.work: George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 20 (London 1884)

summary.en: The four children of Pulotu - Ua (Rain), Fan (Long grass), Langi (Heavens) and Tala (Story) - visit Papatea in the east; Ua is struck on the neck (hence taua, war), Fan is trodden, Langi is spat upon, Tala escapes. Elo, king of Pulotu, makes the first war in history, sweeping Papatea clean; from its refugees come the names Tutuila, Upolu and Savaii.
summary.zh: 普洛圖四子——雨、長草、天、故事——東訪帕帕特亞：雨被打頸（戰爭一詞tauua之源），草被踐踏，天被唾面，故事獨得脫身。普洛圖王埃洛興師問罪，史稱第一戰，掃滅帕帕特亞；其遺民之名合成群島之名——圖圖伊拉、烏波盧、薩瓦伊。

sensitivity.note: Duplicate-thread record retained for motif-cluster indexing of the war-origin legend.

passages.text: The four children of Head of Day and Tail of Day - Ua, or Rain; Fan, Long grass; Langi, Heavens; and Tala, or Story - went to visit Papatea in the east. The Papateans heard of the arrival of the four brothers and determined to kill them: first Ua was struck on the neck, and hence the word taua, or beat the neck, as the word for war - this was the beginning of wars; others stood on the neck of Fan, and hence the proverb in war, 'To-morrow we shall tread on the neck of Fan'; others surrounded and spat on Langi, and hence the proverb for ill-usage, 'It is spitting on Langi'; Tala was spared, and escaped uninjured.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 20 (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Elo, the king of Pulotu, was enraged and prepared to go and fight the Papateans - this was the first war in history; they went, they fought, they conquered, and made a clean sweep of Papatea, and hence the proverb, 'Like the rage of Elo'. All who fled to the bush were sought and killed; only those who fled to sea escaped: Tutu and Ila reached Tutuila, U and Polu reached Upolu, Sa and Vaila reached Savaii - islands named by the union of the names of the survivors of the first war of the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Turner, Samoa A Hundred Years Ago and Long Before, ch. 20 (1884); not verbatim.
